# Xteink Shopify store snapshots

Dated, machine-readable captures of `xteink.com`'s public Shopify endpoints. **Primary
evidence** for every pricing, SKU, variant, stock and launch-date claim in the Xteink device
records.

> **Promoted out of `archive/devices/xteink/shared-artifacts/research-scratch/` on 2026-09-20.** These files were the *only* local copy of
> the evidence behind ~15 cited source rows, and they sat in a working directory. They are small
> (880 KB for both snapshots) and **cannot be re-fetched** — a live storefront has no history —
> so they are kept in the repository rather than archived.

## Why a store snapshot is primary evidence

`xteink.com` is a stock Shopify store, so these endpoints answer unauthenticated and return
structured data rather than prose:

| Endpoint | Gives |
|---|---|
| `/products.json?limit=250&page=N` | the whole catalogue: title, handle, `published_at`, `created_at`, variants, per-variant SKU, price and `available` |
| `/collections.json` | every collection and its handle |
| `/collections/<handle>/products.json?limit=250` | membership of one collection |

This matters because **the vendor's own product prose is demonstrably unreliable** — the X3
listing advertises "adjustable warm light settings" and "Cloud sync", and the X3 has neither.
The JSON is generated by the platform, not written by marketing.

⚠ **`body_html` can be empty.** The X4 Classic's entire specification table exists *only* in the
rendered product page, not in `/products.json`. An agent reading the JSON alone concludes the
vendor published no specifications at all. The rendered page is kept beside the device it
describes:
[`devices/xteink/x4-classic/artifacts/x4-classic-product-page-2026-09-11.html`](../../../../devices/xteink/x4-classic/artifacts/x4-classic-product-page-2026-09-11.html).

## The two snapshots

| Directory | Retrieved | Files | Bytes | What it establishes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| [`2026-09-04/`](2026-09-04/) | **2026-09-04** | 13 | 321,478 | 23 products. X3 $69, X4 Pro $99. **The X4 is delisted** — its collection holds accessories only, all sold out. The `x4-classic` collection exists but holds **4 accessories and no device** |
| [`2026-09-11/`](2026-09-11/) | **2026-09-11** | 16 | 528,398 | **The X4 Classic launch**: `published_at` `2026-09-06T19:57:20-07:00`, US$79.00, SKUs `X4Classic-gray` / `-black`, four bundle SKUs at $95, `available: true`. The `machine` collection — the vendor's device line-up — is **exactly three**: X3 $69, X4 Classic $79, X4 Pro $99, with the X4 absent |

Having **two dated snapshots one week apart** is what makes the launch claim evidential rather
than assertional: the same endpoint, before and after, showing a collection gaining a device.

`products-p2.json` / `products-p3.json` are 15-byte empty-page responses in both snapshots.
They are retained deliberately — they prove pagination was followed to exhaustion, rather than
the catalogue being truncated at page 1.

## ⚠ A directory-name trap, and how it was resolved

The 2026-09-11 snapshot was fetched into a scratch directory named **`vendor-2026-09-07/`**,
after the date given in that session's task brief. **Three independent remote sources put the
real retrieval date at 2026-09-11 or later**: the host clock, every Shopify record's
`updated_at` (`2026-09-11T15:52:09-07:00`), and a dated Judge.me review
(`2026-09-08 04:57:34 UTC`).

**The directory here is named for the true retrieval date, 2026-09-11**, and all citing records
use that date. The scratch directory keeps its misleading name because it is referenced from
that session's own log; the discrepancy is documented in
[`devices/xteink/x4-classic/research-log.md`](../../../../devices/xteink/x4-classic/research-log.md) §0.

**Never take a retrieval date from a directory name.** Take it from the data.

## Reacquisition

`automatic`, but **the result will differ** — these are live-commerce snapshots, and that is the
point of keeping them. To take a fresh one:

```bash
D=$(date +%F); mkdir -p "$D"
for p in 1 2 3; do
  curl -s "https://xteink.com/products.json?limit=250&page=$p" -o "$D/products-p$p.json"
done
curl -s "https://xteink.com/collections.json" -o "$D/collections.json"
python3 -c "
import json;print('\n'.join(c['handle'] for c in json.load(open('$D/collections.json'))['collections']))" |
while read h; do
  curl -s "https://xteink.com/collections/$h/products.json?limit=250" -o "$D/coll-$h.json"
done
```

`executed-success` — this is the method both snapshots used. No authentication, no UA
substitution needed; a plain request works.
